# How to update Composer in Windows 10

When you run `composer update` on a Windows 10 machine and receive a warning about an outdated version, it usually points to a mismatch between your current installation method and the command you are executing. The specific scenario described involves a setup using XAMPP where the executable resides at `C:/ProgramData/ComposerSetup/bin/composer.phar`. This path indicates that Composer was installed via a legacy installer script rather than being added directly to your system's PATH environment variable.

The core issue stems from how Windows handles local file paths versus global commands. When you execute `composer.phar update` or `php composer.phar update`, the shell attempts to run the version currently residing in your working directory, not the one installed by the Composer Setup script. Since that directory likely does not contain a valid executable, the command fails immediately. Similarly, invoking it with `composer C:/ProgramData/ComposerSetup/bin/composer.phar update` fails because the `composer` binary itself is missing from your system path; only the `.phar` file exists at that specific location.

To resolve this, you must first ensure you are targeting the correct executable. The most reliable method on Windows is to use the full absolute path in conjunction with the PHP interpreter or the command-line tool if it exists globally. If you have downloaded the standalone installer (the `.exe` version) alongside the script-based install, that binary would typically be located in `C:\ProgramData\ComposerSetup\bin`.

Run the following command to trigger the self-updater for that specific installation:

```cmd
php "C:/ProgramData/ComposerSetup/bin/composer.phar" self-update
```

Alternatively, if you have added the Composer installer directory to your system PATH, you can run `composer self-update` from any terminal. This is generally preferred because it keeps your working directory clean and allows you to use the shorter command syntax throughout your project lifecycle.

If the self-updater fails with a 403 Forbidden error or similar network issues, it often means the local installation has been blocked by Composer's security protocols or that the underlying PHP version bundled with XAMPP is incompatible with the latest Composer release. The legacy Composer Setup script often bundles an older version of PHP or relies on system defaults that may differ from your project requirements.

In cases where `composer.phar` refuses to update, you should verify the PHP version compatibility. Modern Composer versions require PHP 8.1 or higher (depending on the exact version installed). If your XAMPP environment is running PHP 7.x, the latest Composer will not run correctly regardless of how you try to update it. You may need to upgrade your XAMPP installation or switch to a standalone PHP distribution that supports the latest runtime versions.

Once the tool is updated successfully, always verify the version by running `composer -V`. If you prefer managing dependencies without relying on the legacy XAMPP stack for Composer, consider downloading the official Windows installer from [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) or the official Laravel site, which provides a more robust integration with modern development workflows. This ensures that your environment remains consistent across different machines and avoids the fragility associated with manual `.phar` file management.
